gf_detail: If this record is the Ningyōchō 福そば, it is a firm no. The noodles are 生麺 made to the shop's own specification by an outside noodle maker and are not jūwari — wheat flour is in the noodle. Udon shares the same boiling water at the same counter. The kakiage and tempura are wheat-battered and deep-fried in a fryer that runs all service. The tsuyu the shop is actually famous for is built on ordinary Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat by default, and the house 辛味噌 is a miso paste with no gluten-free claim attached. No gluten-free item, no wheat-free handling, and a standing counter gives a kitchen no room to run a separate line.
vegan_detail: The tsuyu is a katsuo/dashi broth — it is the whole point of the shop — so even a plain kake soba is not vegan. The kakiage is vegetable but shares a fryer with prawn tempura, and the popular sides are 出汁巻き玉子 (egg) and 温玉. There is no plant-based tsuyu on offer.

chef_bio.chef_name: Yun (雲さん) — given only as a surname in the sources
chef_bio.origin: Xiamen, China; resident in Japan for over twenty years at the time of the 2020 profile
chef_bio.background: Written about the Ningyōchō 福そば, which is a real and well-documented shop — but the tie to this light record is a name match and nothing more, so read it as background on a candidate, not as this record's biography. Bungei Shunjū profiled the owner in February 2020 under the headline 「日本在住23年 中国人留学生が『日本そばの達人』になり、東京に名店を」: a Chinese student who came to Japan, worked in Japanese restaurants, and fell for soba by way of the tsuyu rather than the noodle. He runs a stand-up counter in Amazake-yokochō that opens before half past seven in the morning, and both the Bunshun piece and favy's 2020 write-up make the same point — that the usual excuses of a standing-soba shop are simply absent here. The noodle is a slightly thin 生麺 ordered to the shop's own specification so that it cooks fast without going slack; the kakiage is fried long and low with air worked into it with chopsticks, and the vegetables rotate with the season (spring chrysanthemum, prawn, lotus root, mushroom); a house-made 辛味噌 is offered as a seasoning. Prices in the 2020 piece ran ¥450–¥460 for tempura soba, ¥100 for a dashimaki, ¥300 for soba-shōchū cut with the hot broth; Tabelog's current budget band is under ¥999 and recent photographs show bowls up to ¥1,000. Cash only, no reservations, all seats non-smoking, standing counter.
chef_bio.philosophy: The broth carries the shop — simple, but with depth; no allowances made for the fact that customers eat standing up.
chef_bio.specialty: Kakiage and squid-tentacle tempura soba; cold soba in summer; dashimaki tamago; a shot of soba-shōchū cut with the hot soba-yu.

anecdotes.text: Bunshun's framing is that a Chinese student who had lived in Japan 23 years became a soba master and opened one of Tokyo's good shops — the hook of the piece is that he came to soba through the tsuyu, not the noodle.
The kakiage is fried at low temperature for a long time, with air pockets deliberately poked into it with chopsticks so it stays crisp under the broth.

Bungei Shunjū (Feb 2020) profiles the Chinese owner and the tsuyu. favy (Nov 2020) gives the owner's origin in Xiamen, the made-to-spec noodle, the kakiage method, the 2020 prices and the then-current 6:40 opening. Retty and several soba blogs corroborate the address and the standing-counter format. Nothing in any source places a 福そば in Shinsen or anywhere in Shibuya-ku.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Standing soba counter: soba and udon go into the same pot, and the tempura fryer runs continuously. Wheat is in the noodle itself, so there is nothing to protect.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The shop's reputation rests on its tsuyu, built on ordinary Japanese soy sauce; no tamari or wheat-free soy is mentioned anywhere.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Bonito dashi in the tsuyu; the shared fryer handles prawn as well as vegetable kakiage; dashimaki and onsen-tamago are among the standard sides.

name: 六厘舎 東京ラーメンストリート店
address_ja: 〒100-0005 東京都千代田区丸の内1-9-1 東京駅一番街 B1F 東京ラーメンストリート内
cuisine: The tsukemen that set off Japan's thick-broth craze — extra-thick noodles dipped in a pork-and-seafood broth simmered down and then crushed by hand until the ingredients lose their shape. Tabelog's budget band is under ¥1,000, and this is the only 六厘舎 that serves a 朝つけめん, from 07:30.
neighborhood: Tokyo Ramen Street, B1 of Tokyo Station Ichibangai on the Yaesu side — inside the station complex, 120 m from Tokyo Station (JR lines and the Marunouchi line); come out of the Yaesu South ticket gate and take the stairs signed 東京駅一番街 before you reach the street.
gf_detail: A firm no, and not a close call. The shop's whole identity is 極太麺 — thick Chinese-style wheat noodles — so wheat is the dish, not a contaminant, and one boiler serves a 26-seat counter. The tsukedare is a long-reduced pork-and-fish broth finished with soy sauce, which contains wheat by default in Japan and is nowhere claimed to be a wheat-free tamari. 松富士食品 does publish an allergen chart for the brand at rokurinsha.com/storage/rokurinsha-allergen.pdf — it was downloaded successfully (HTTP 200, 685 KB) but is a scanned/outlined PDF whose text could not be extracted here, so its contents are NOT being reported. Nothing on the brand site, on Tabelog or on the Tokyo Station Ichibangai listing offers a gluten-free noodle or any wheat-free handling.
vegan_detail: No. The broth is animal on both axes — pork bones plus fish, with a 魚粉 finish that is part of the house style — and the standard bowls carry chāshū and a marinated egg. There is no plant-based broth, no vegan bowl, and no way to have the noodles without the dipping broth.

chef_bio.chef_name: 三田遼斉 (Mita; the given name is written 遼斉 on Japanese Wikipedia and 遼生 in some ramen blogs, so treat the reading as unsettled)
chef_bio.origin: Ōsaki, Shinagawa-ku, Tokyo — where the first shop opened
chef_bio.background: 六厘舎 opened on 18 April 2005 as a single shop in Ōsaki, Shinagawa-ku, and very nearly failed: the first months were quiet enough that Japanese Wikipedia calls it 危機的状況. What saved it was the founder abandoning the safe recipe for the one he actually wanted — 超濃厚スープ・極太麺, an ultra-concentrated broth with extra-thick noodles. Magazines and television picked it up, it took the tsukemen prize at TOKYO1週間's ramen-of-the-year awards in both 2006 and 2007, and the queue became the story: routinely more than a hundred people, a standard wait of about two hours, two and a half hours or more over long weekends. The queue is also what killed the original shop — the neighbours had had enough and no fix was in sight, so the Ōsaki honten closed on 29 August 2010, with people queueing overnight for the last 350 bowls. The brand survived through its branches, including this Tokyo Station shop, which had opened on 17 June 2009. The honten came back one day a week from January 2012 (Saturdays only), then reopened properly at Ōsaki With City on 18 April 2014 — the founding anniversary, to the day. A fire near that dining room's air conditioner on 9 March 2015 shut it for eight months; it reopened on 27 November 2015. The house style is described on the company's own About page as 「ガサツで荒々しく男らしいつけめん」 — rough, unrefined, masculine — and the broth is made by simmering a large volume of ingredients for a long time and then crushing them by hand until they lose their form, to pull out the last of the umami. The brand is run by 株式会社松富士食品 of 千代田区内神田2-2-5, incorporated in November 2008 against a founding date of 18 April 2005, which also operates 舎鈴, トナリ, ジャンクガレッジ and 次念序; in December 2025 松屋フーズホールディングス bought its parent 松富士 outright, for about ¥9.1 billion, to expand into tsukemen, completing on 5 January 2026. Whether the founder is still in the kitchen is not stated in anything that was read, and is not claimed here.
chef_bio.philosophy: 「ガサツで荒々しく男らしいつけめん」 — deliberately rough and unrefined; and 現在進行形の味, a flavour still being adjusted, so the company is explicit that today's bowl is not the founding recipe.
chef_bio.specialty: つけめん and 特製つけめん with the ultra-thick noodles; 味玉つけめん; 生七味つけめん; 中華そば; and, only at this branch, 特製朝つけめん served from 07:30.

anecdotes.text: The Ōsaki original shut on 29 August 2010 purely because of its own queue — over a hundred people at a time, a two-hour standard wait, and neighbours who could no longer live with it. People queued overnight for the last 350 bowls.
It reopened at Ōsaki With City on 18 April 2014 — the anniversary of the 2005 founding, to the day.
The broth is not merely simmered: after hours in the pot the ingredients are crushed by hand until they lose their form, which is how the company describes getting the last of the umami out.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The brand site rokurinsha.com carries the house style and the menu, and its About page gives the 「ガサツで荒々しく」 line and the hand-crushing method. The operator's store locator (shop.mtfj.co.jp/stores/61) gives this branch as 六厘舎 東京ラーメンストリート店, 〒100-0005 東京都千代田区丸の内1-9-1 東京駅一番街B1F, 03-3286-0166, 07:30–09:45 and 10:00–23:00 every day of the week. Tokyo Station Ichibangai's own shop page repeats the B1 Tokyo Ramen Street location, the phone number and the two service periods, and calls out the morning tsukemen. Tabelog 13093047 gives 26 seats (10 counter, 8 across two-tops), 120 m from Tokyo Station, opened 17 June 2009, budget under ¥999, cash plus transport e-money, and a run of ラーメン TOKYO 百名店 selections from 2017 through 2025. Japanese Wikipedia, read from the raw wikitext, supplies the founder, the 2005-04-18 founding in Ōsaki, the TOKYO1週間 awards, the 2010 closure and its cause, the 2014 reopening, the 2015 fire, the corporate details of 松富士食品 and the 2025–26 松屋フーズ acquisition.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat is the product, not a trace: 極太麺 are thick wheat noodles and one boiler serves the whole 26-seat counter. There is no gluten-free noodle and no separate line.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The dipping broth is finished with soy sauce; no tamari or wheat-free soy is mentioned on the brand site, the operator's store page or Tabelog.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Pork-and-fish broth with a fish-powder finish, chāshū and marinated egg on the standard bowls. Nothing on the menu is animal-free.

staff_allergy_handling.text: An allergen chart PDF is published for the brand and was retrieved successfully, but it is a scanned/outlined document whose text could not be extracted, so no claim is made about what it says. Treat the link as something to open on a phone at the counter, not as an assurance.

positives.text: Ticket-machine ordering and a managed queue mean no negotiation in Japanese is needed — which cuts both ways: easy to order, but nobody to ask about ingredients mid-service.

cultural_comfort.note: About as approachable as a famous Tokyo ramen shop gets: it is inside Tokyo Station, signposted in English along Tokyo Ramen Street, and you queue, choose from the pictures while you wait, then buy a ticket from the machine before sitting. Staff hand out aprons so the thick broth does not ruin your shirt, and one first-timer's account records a 23-minute wait behind about twenty people at 1:15 pm. Regular size is filling; large is a lot. Cash or transport IC (Suica and the like); Tabelog lists no credit cards. 26 seats, so it is a counter meal, not a table to linger at.

enrich_note: CONFIRMED. The light record's 六厘舎 / 丸の内・東京駅 / つけ麺 is right on every count; what it lacked was the branch and the address. 六厘舎 has five Tokyo locations (Ōsaki, Tokyo Station, Skytree Solamachi, Haneda, Ueno), and the one at this pin is 六厘舎 東京ラーメンストリート店 at 千代田区丸の内1-9-1, Tokyo Station Ichibangai B1 — verified against the operator's own store locator, the Tokyo Station Ichibangai shop page and Tabelog 13093047, all of which agree on the address, the phone number (03-3286-0166) and the two daily service periods. The name field has been made branch-specific for that reason; this is a disambiguation, not a name correction. Coordinates moved from the neighbourhood centroid to the Tokyo Ramen Street food court itself (OpenStreetMap node 4646514992, 35.68038 / 139.76788); loc_precise is now true. GF is a hard no — thick wheat noodles are the dish. The brand's allergen PDF was fetched successfully but is unreadable as text, so nothing is asserted from it.

chef_bio.background: Could not be established, because 象本店 is not the name of any restaurant in Japan. Tabelog's nationwide free-word search for 象本店 returns only fuzzy matches on the 本店 half — 源蔵本店 (Hiroshima), 半蔵 本店 (Kanagawa), 大名酒蔵 本店 (Osaka), とりぞう 本店 (Ōita, a yakitori shop and the only nationwide hit whose name even reads ぞう) — and nothing called 象本店. Gnavi's nationwide free-word search returns exactly two results for the string, 象印食堂 大阪本店 and 象の耳 用賀本店, neither of them a yakitori house and neither in Shimbashi. Recorded for the file, because this record will read as a generic invitation to eat soba in Shimbashi: Japanese soba is not a gluten-free food. Standard nihachi noodles are 20 percent wheat flour, even 十割 noodles are rolled on a board dusted with 打ち粉 wheat flour, the tsuyu is wheat soy sauce, and every standing counter in Shimbashi boils soba and udon in the same water and runs a tempura fryer all service.
